Photograph: Axel Schmidt/Reuters Germany Analysis The Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for Europe Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Initial evidence suggests aerial drone, found near Ukrainian cargo planes at German airport, came from Russia Wed 5 Aug 2026 13.32 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 14.53 EDT Share The armed drone found at Leipzig airport on Wednesday may not have exploded, but the fact that it got inside the perimeter, close to Ukrainian cargo planes , raises obvious concerns for the security of international aviation. Though the identity of the culprits is unknown, the initial evidence points firmly towards a Russian-orchestrated plot. It is the first time that a drone with explosives has been found in Europe far from the Ukrainian border. Photographs published by German newspapers show a quadcopter, a design familiar from the Ukraine war, with a package attached. It lies a few metres short of a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane, with its easily identifiable yellow and blue trim livery. Police from the German state of Saxony confirmed that the drone was “carrying an unknown explosive device” discovered by an employee in the “secure cargo flight operations area” near the airport’s southern runway. German media reported the attached bomb was made of PETN and semtex plastic explosive – the second of the two being the munition that exploded inside Pan Am 103 over Lockerbie. But the bomb attached to the drone did not explode, because the detonator was faulty. A local newspaper, Leipziger Volkszeitung, said police discovered as much as 800g of explosive. This would be “enough to do considerable damage” to a plane, according to Trevor Lawrence, an explosives expert with Cranfield University, not least because “aeroplane bodies are ridiculously thin, often only 3mm aluminium”. Whether the explosive was specifically semtex, invented in the Czech Republic, or from another country may not have been determined. But any type of plastic explosive has typically only been available to militaries or well-established terror groups, not to reckless amateur drone pilots messing around. A second unidentified flying object, which could well have been another drone, also collided with a DHL cargo plane in the aftermath of the first incident several hundred metres above the ground. The cargo plane only sustained minor damage. Leipzig airport is a sensitive site, the European base of Ukrainian Antonov jets, used for heavy cargo. The airport is also used by Nato and the German military for transport, as well as being a DHL hub, and the Ukrainian planes suggest it may also have been a node for supplies to Kyiv. Nato would only say it was aware of the incident on Wednesday, though it is eye-catching that the western alliance appears to have not been able to prevent drones from flying into and over a strategic airport. It is not the first time Leipzig airport has been involved in a dangerous incident. A firebomb, posted via DHL, exploded at the airport in July 2024 while a second travelled to the UK and caught fire at a warehouse in Birmingham . Two similar packages were also found in Poland. A subsequent pan-European investigation identified 22 suspects in Lithuania and Poland who are suspected of having been employed by Russian intelligence. The investigation found perpetrators were recruited and given instructions online, and frequently paid in cryptocurrency, their knowledge of the full plot apparently limited. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion Russia has also been behind a string of drone incursions into Europe over the past year, some more blatant than others. Around 20 unarmed Russian delta-wing Gerbera drones crossed into Poland last September , forcing a major alert, with people in two of the country’s eastern provinces told to shelter indoors. An analysis by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) thinktank concluded last month that the Kremlin was behind a concerted drone surveillance campaign that targeted the US airbase at RAF Lakenheath and other key military sites in France, Belgium and the Netherlands. In the first case, Nato jets struggled to shoot down the incoming drones, most of which eventually crashed or lost power and glided to the ground. In the second, western militaries struggled to work out who were the culprits, failing to capture any of the drones or react to the surveillance efforts promptly. Russia, in sum, has so far been able to conduct other firebomb operations, as well as drone harassment and surveillance campaigns with relative impunity. Moscow is already subject to a wide range of sanctions following the invasion of Ukraine, and it is likely to believe that the west has little more it is willing to punish the country with. “A drone carrying a charge with a detonator that failed is a different proposition to what we have seen before,” said Charlie Edwards, a senior fellow with the IISS, adding ominously: “It is likely, though not yet certain, that this was intended to function rather than to be found.” Explore more on these topics Germany Ukraine Russia Europe analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.jns.org/opinion/michael-freu.text: More than eight decades ago, amid the Holocaust in Poland, a rabbi looked at a Jewish child beside a Torah scroll and saw the Jewish future. Three years ago, Simchat Torah changed forever. On the morning of Oct. 7, 2023, as Jews across Israel were preparing to celebrate the completion of the annual Torah-reading cycle, Hamas terrorists poured in from the Gaza Strip, murdering 1,200 Israelis and taking 251 others hostage. Suddenly, a holiday associated with dancing became one of slaughter. For many Jews, that has made Simchat Torah one of the most emotionally complicated days on the calendar. How do you dance on the anniversary of a massacre? How do you sing when the date itself summons memories of young people hunted down at the Nova music festival, families murdered in their homes and communities along the Gaza border overrun? An answer can be found in another Simchat Torah, more than 80 years ago, in the Warsaw Ghetto in 1942. The Germans had begun the mass deportation of Warsaw’s Jews to Treblinka. More than a quarter of a million had been sent to their deaths. Of the roughly 400,000 Jews who had once been crowded into the ghetto, perhaps 60,000 remained. Yet when the Jewish holidays arrived, some Jews in the ghetto insisted on observing them. Dr. Hillel Seidman, a religious Jew who kept a remarkable diary of life inside the ghetto, recorded what happened on Simchat Torah. About 15 men gathered in the apartment of the great Torah scholar Rabbi Menachem Ziemba at 37 Nalewki Street. They took Torah scrolls in their arms and began the traditional hakafot, circling the room. But there was little joy. Among those present was Rabbi Yehuda Leib Orlean, a prominent Gerrer Chassid and Torah scholar. His wife and five children had been murdered. Seidman described him as utterly broken. The men began reciting the familiar Simchat Torah verses, but instead of singing them exuberantly, they intoned them mournfully. Then something unexpected happened: a 12-year-old Jewish boy entered the room. The sight itself was extraordinary. By then, almost no Jewish children remained in the ghetto. Children had been among the first targets of the Nazi killing machine. Rabbi Orlean saw the boy, grabbed him and pulled him close to the Torah scroll he was holding. And then the shattered rabbi began to dance. A yunger Yid mit di heilige Toyreh! he cried out in Yiddish. (“A young Jew with the holy Torah!”) Again and again, he sang the words as he danced with the child. The men around him began to weep. Then they joined in, forming a circle around the rabbi and the boy. Seidman would later describe it as the final dance of the final Simchat Torah celebrated by the Jews of the Warsaw Ghetto. Warsaw in the fall of 1942 and Israel in 2023 are not the same, and they should not be equated. The Jews trapped in the ghetto were stateless and defenseless, surrounded by an enemy systematically exterminating them. Israel is a sovereign Jewish state with an army capable of striking back. But the two moments confront us with a similar question: What is Jewish joy when everything around us seems to argue against it? Rabbi Orlean’s answer was remarkable precisely because he wasn’t pretending that everything was fine. His world had been devastated. His dance did not erase his grief. And yet, he saw a Jewish child standing beside a Torah scroll and understood that this was something the Germans had not yet managed to destroy: the possibility of a Jewish future. Last year, on Simchat Torah in 2025, hundreds of people, including Israeli soldiers, gathered at the site of the Nova festival, where so many young Israelis had been murdered. They carried a Torah scroll and danced, singing Am Yisrael Chai, “the nation of Israel lives.” The place where Jews had been hunted while celebrating just two years previously became a place where Jews once again danced. None of this makes the losses disappear. There will be empty places in countless homes and synagogues this Simchat Torah. There will be parents without children, children without parents, and families who will never again experience the holiday as they once did. We will remember them. But we will dance. Not because we have forgotten Oct. 7, but because we remember what Rabbi Orlean understood in Warsaw. More than eight decades ago, he looked at a Jewish child beside a Torah scroll and saw something worth dancing for: the Jewish future. This Simchat Torah, after everything the Jewish people have endured these past three years, perhaps that is what we should see as well. A young Jew with the holy Torah. And the Jewish story continuing.

Authorities say the dead on Saturday included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio acknowledged an American citizen had been killed. U.S. President Donald Trump calls the attack unacceptable. A Saudi-led coalition blamed Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen. The attack is the latest of several in the past week on King Khalid International Airport. The Houthis claimed the others. The attack is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies for military support. DOJ says it's investigating whether White House TV pool's coverage halt violated antitrust law WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. Department of Justice is investigating whether the decision of the White House television press pool to halt coverage of President Donald Trump last month violated antitrust law. Emily Covington, a department spokesperson, says group boycotts among business competitors might violate U.S. law. The television pool of five broadcasters last month ceased presidential coverage after the administration barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. Messages were sent late Saturday to the five outlets seeking comment. The White House press pool, which is a rotating cast of news outlets that covers the president, has become a proxy for the wider fight over press freedom. 4 dead from storm as Isaias brings threat of floods across the Southeast PANAMA CITY BEACH, Fla. (AP) — At least four people died after the first hurricane of the Atlantic season roared onto the Florida Panhandle and carved a path into the Southeast. Isaias left behind a trail of damaged roofs and downed power lines along the Gulf Coast. The storm continues to bring heavy rain and the threat of flash floods across the region. Isaias came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane on Friday near Destin, Florida. Hurricane-force winds tore the roofs off a Pensacola hotel. And the city's mayor says the airport “took some damage.” Two people died when trees fell onto homes in Florida and Alabama. Puerto Vallarta boards up as Hurricane Simon hits Category 4 strength PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico (AP) — Hurricane Simon has strengthened into a powerful Category 4 storm as it barrels toward Mexico’s coast. The National Hurricane Center in Miami reports Simon’s maximum sustained winds have increased to 150 mph. The center expects Simon to be near or just inland of Mexico's west-central coast on Sunday. The hurricane could bring up to 30 inches of rain to parts of southwestern Mexico, causing life-threatening flooding and mudslides. Jalisco state has suspended classes and begun evacuations in at-risk areas. Businesses in Puerto Vallarta are boarding up windows as the storm approaches. Shooting leaves 9 dead including suspect in Erie, Pennsylvania, police say Authorities say a man killed eight people including a pregnant woman, children and other relatives at his home in Erie, Pennsylvania. He then took his own life. Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah says the 45-year-old man was related to seven of the victims in Friday’s shooting. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman. Lorah said at a news conference Saturday that video and audio evidence reviewed by investigators show two distressed women arriving at the home and pounding at the door. Then the gunman emerged and shot them. The other victims were found inside the home. Trump says Ukraine should get a new president as he blames Zelenskyy for US diesel prices WASHINGTON (AP) — Former President Donald Trump says Ukraine needs a new leader, suggesting President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hasn't done enough to end the war with Russia. Speaking at the White House on Saturday, Trump said Zelenskyy has lost 30% of Ukraine and millions have died. He also claimed the war wouldn't have started if he had been president in 2022. Meanwhile, Russian strikes killed at least 20 people in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region on Saturday. Ukrainian officials expressed anger over Trump's recent deal to buy Russian diesel, warning it could help fund Moscow's war efforts. Christa Pike is discharged from a hospital after surviving execution attempt, her attorneys say NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection, has been moved back to prison. That is according to a statement by her attorneys released Saturday. The statement says Pike is back at the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years. Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state attempted to execute her by lethal injection on Sept. 30 for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike had been in a hospital since the failed execution. The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said what went wrong. Panama declares a state of emergency as powerful quake aftershocks rattle communities LA VILLA DE LOS SANTOS, Panama (AP) — Panama's government has declared a state of emergency following two powerful earthquakes that shook the country. The quakes, with magnitudes of 7.7 and 6.6, caused damage across all 10 provinces and two Indigenous territories. Officials report no deaths but note injuries and significant structural damage. The earthquakes struck Friday, leading to evacuations and more than 100 aftershocks. Most damage occurred in the central provinces. Rising sea levels prompted evacuations on Isla Caña. The U.S. has pledged $5 million in humanitarian aid, and other countries have offered support. The Panama Canal remains operational. Pope Leo declares death penalty 'inadmissible' as his native US plans to livestream execution ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV has declared capital punishment "inadmissible.” He has penned a social media post for the World Day Against the Death Penalty, as his native United States announced plans to livestream an execution by firing squad. The American pope quoted the revised Catholic teaching on capital punishment ushered in by Pope Francis. The Argentine pontiff had decreed in 2018 that the death penalty is unacceptable because it attacks the inherent dignity of a human being. Leo on Saturday wrote that the common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment. A third school attack in less than a week shakes Poland WARSAW, Poland (AP) — Police say a woman wounded three people at a school in Warsaw, Poland. It is the third school attack in less than a week. The victims were attacked while submitting papers at the school office. The suspect used a "dangerous object" to attack a 17-year-old girl and two others. None of the injuries were life-threatening. Earlier in the week, two other attacks occurred in central Poland, shocking the nation. Authorities have detained 76 people and checked nearly 50,000 schools to prevent further violence. The government is implementing extra security measures and considering new legislation to block harmful online content. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. https://www.cp24.com/news/canada/2026/11.text: EDMONTON, Alta.- As Canadians mark Remembrance Day, one father is remembering his 26-year-old son, Sgt. Morgan Wong. Morgan was among four Canadian soldiers killed in a training fire at CFB Wainwright last month. Dozens of others were injured, leaving families across the country facing an uncertain road ahead. “Sometimes, I just feel like he’s still on training,” said Morgan’s father, Chek Wong. “But when the reality hits ... he’s not coming back.” For Chek, the tragedy compounded his family’s loss. His wife, Hong Tan, died of lung cancer in 2020, leaving him to raise their two children, Morgan and his sister, without her. Now, six years later, he is mourning their son. “Losing him, it’s just like ... take a part of me,” Chek said, struggling to find the words. “I’ll stay strong for my daughter ... family.” Victims in care The impact of the fire isstill being felt in Alberta hospitals. According to Acute Care Alberta, 21 patients injured in the CFB Wainwright fire remained in hospital as of Nov. 6, including nine in critical condition. The Canadian Armed Forces is sending 15 registered nurses with specialized burn and intensive care training to Alberta to help care for the injured. The nurses are expected to arrive beginning Nov. 10 and remain until Jan. 15, 2027. “This offers well-deserved respite to civilian staff who have been working around the clock to provide this highly specialized care,” Acute Care Alberta said in an emailed statement. A late-night knock For Chek, the events that changed his family forever began with an unexpected knock at the door. Three military officers had arrived at his Edmonton home late at night. “I peeked out the window,” he recalled. “That’s not a good sign.” He remembers wishing it were all a dream. His partner, Kelly Fairweather, said Chek was overwhelmed by the news. “I just remember ... him passing me his phone and saying, ‘I don’t know who to call. I don’t know what to do next.’” Fairweather said family members and friends have been helping Chek navigate the weeks since Morgan’s death. Some of Morgan’s closest friends have continued visiting, sharing memories and stories that occasionally bring laughter amid the sadness. To those who knew him, Morgan was a reserved young man who revealed a different side of himself around the people he loved. “Morgan is (a) very quiet person. But if you know him, he (opens) up and is really nice,” Chek said. Chek also remembers the little things, like preparing home-cooked meals for Morgan before he left for work and when he returned home. “He loved the curry,” Chek recalled. “He really enjoyed almost all those homemade food things (he) can’t get anywhere else.” His father remembers a son who cared deeply for others and was always willing to help. Morgan volunteered with St. John Ambulance and developed an interest in military service while still in school. A ‘remarkable’ soldier Chek recalled Morgan coming home at 17 and expressing an interest in joining the army reserve. “I was like ‘well, let him try. Let’s give him a chance. It’s an opportunity he likes to do ... he likes to serve his country.’ Well, I said go for it,” Chek recalled. Over the years, that interest developed into a career of service that made his father immensely proud. “He was a remarkable soldier and a great leader,” Chek said. “He liked to help people and he’s very genuine.” Morgan was also a newlywed. He met his wife, Laura Karzinina, in Riga, Latvia, while deployed overseas. The couple married in December 2025, less than a year before his death. “We haven’t had a big wedding yet, so we just had an intimate ceremony with his dad and his friends,” Karzinina recalled. For Morgan’s uncle, George, who travelled from Hong Kong to support his brother and the family, the news was almost impossible to comprehend. He recalled being on a street in Hong Kong when he received the call. “I couldn’t believe it,” he said. “I lived in denial for a couple of days.” George also reflected on Morgan’s deployment to Latvia. “On the one hand, I’m concerned. But on the other hand, I’m very proud because there is the Wong name representing NATO,” he recalled. Neighbours come to help As the Wong family navigates its grief, neighbours and community organizations have been finding ways to show their support. Former Edmonton city councillor Jennifer Rice helped organize a community gathering on Oct. 22. Residents brought flowers, signed cards and shared their condolences with Chek and his loved ones. Rice said the response extended beyond those who personally knew the family, with local organizations and community members offering help. Community members have also rallied online to provide financial support to the Wong family. “I need the family [to] know ... they’re not alone. They have the community behind them,” Rice said. She said that continued support will be important in the months ahead. The Legacy of Peace Society is also planning a commemorative tree planting in Morgan’s honour, with hopes that members of the public will be able to participate. Morgan’s former elementary school also held a Remembrance Day ceremony Tuesday, which Chek and his family attended. Chek described the ceremony as beautiful and touching, particularly because it took place at a school where his son had once been a student. Despite his own grief, Chek said he continues to think about the other military families whose lives were changed by the fire. “My heart goes to the family ... all the families that are impacted by this tragedy,” he said through tears. He hopes they can find comfort in supporting one another through the difficult months ahead. Chek hopes his son will be remembered for his service and everything he accomplished. “I want everybody to ... remember him as a hero, that he was serving his country,” he said.
